issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a rape trauma profile, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the only item that implies perpetration or morally troubling behaviour by the patient. Paired with memory items centered on terror and shame and trigger items tied to tiredness, driving with others, and sounds, this appraisal is hard to reconcile clinically with the rest of the profile and with the trauma type. The other negative appraisals reflect mistrust and loss of faith, which fit sexual assault trauma; this item instead points toward a different moral injury formulation and creates an internal mismatch within the Negative Appraisals node.

vignette:
Raymond, a 53-year-old married bus driver of North American background, came to treatment after more than a year of feeling that his life had narrowed around one night he could not escape. The assault happened after a late shift, when he was already exhausted and had agreed to give a coworker a ride home. He remembered the ordinary weight of the evening at first — the bus emptying out, the low hum of the engine, the radio crackling faintly — and then the sudden terror of being overpowered and raped. What has stayed with him most is not only what happened, but how vividly it comes back. Certain sounds and the deep fatigue he felt after those shifts did not just remind Raymond of the assault; they pulled him back into it, and the memory would arrive with such force that he felt as if the night were happening again. Once that happened, he would immediately read the world through the assault, concluding that anywhere he was tired, exposed, or surrounded by other people was a place where he could be hurt without warning. When he remembers it, he said, it is not like thinking about an old event; it is as if the same terror returns in his body, and the memory runs through his mind like a film that will not stop playing. Certain sounds can still pull him straight back into it, especially noises that resemble the sounds from that night, and when he is already tired the recollection feels even closer, more immediate, as if fatigue leaves less distance between the present and the past.

In the weeks that followed, Raymond found himself watching for any sign that something similar could happen again. He had come to believe that people cannot be trusted and that whatever faith he had once placed in others, in life, or in a higher power had been badly broken. Because he had come to believe that others were dangerous and that the world had failed him, even ordinary noises on the bus — a sudden laugh, a scuffle near the back, the metallic click of a seatbelt — took on the meaning of danger for him, as if each one could be the start of another assault. Those same moments did not simply unsettle him; they confirmed the thought that nowhere was truly safe and that he had to stay on guard every time he drove. He was ashamed of what had happened to his body, and that shame colored the way he thought about the assault and about himself. Because of that, he became wary in situations that reminded him of the attack. Driving with others, once part of his job and something he had done without thought, now felt unsafe and exposing; being seated behind the wheel with a passenger nearby made him scan the seats, mirrors, and faces with a vigilance that left him tense and uneasy. Related sounds on the bus — a sudden laugh, a scuffle near the back, the metallic click of a seatbelt, a tone that echoed the night of the assault — could make him feel cornered before he had time to reason with himself. Those moments were not just reminders; they fed his mistrust, confirming for him that other people might turn dangerous without warning, and that he could not count on anyone to protect him.

That mistrust then shaped the way the memory itself returned. When the memory came back with that same terror attached, it made the bus and the people on it feel newly threatening, so that even neutral sounds or a passenger shifting in a seat became warnings he could not ignore. The more vividly the assault returned to him, the more he searched for signs of danger around him, and the more easily he found them. When Raymond noticed a passenger behind him, or heard a sound that resembled the assault, his mind would snap back to the event with the same terror attached. He described the recollection as if it arrived whole, not softened by time, bringing back the humiliation and fear together. The shame on recall was especially painful: remembering did not simply mean reliving the violence, but confronting what had been done to his body and the sense that he had been left altered by it. In those moments he would become even more alert to possible danger, listening harder, looking more often in the mirrors, and bracing for the next sign that someone could hurt him again. The more he searched for threat, the more the bus and the people on it felt charged with it.

Over months, Raymond began arranging his life around these moments. He tried to avoid being tired because exhaustion made the memories sharper, but his work schedule often left him drained anyway, and on those days the echoes came more easily. He started taking routes and breaks with more caution, and his interactions with riders became clipped and guarded. The changes at work were obvious enough that his wife noticed he came home worn down and withdrawn, as if he had spent the day fighting something invisible. He was embarrassed that he could no longer occupy the role of the steady professional he had once taken pride in. At home, he carried the same belief that people could not be trusted, and that belief kept the circle tight: the less safe others seemed, the more he monitored them; the more he monitored, the more often he noticed the sounds and situations that stirred the memory; and each return of the memory deepened his shame and conviction that the world was no longer dependable.

By the time he sought help, Raymond was frightened by how completely the assault had shaped the way he moved through his days. He had reached a point where he was most afraid that driving tired, with passengers behind him and the wrong sound in the bus, would pull him back into the terror again and again, and he was also afraid that he would keep retreating from other people until distrust became the only way he knew how to live. He came to treatment hoping to find some way to sit in the driver’s seat, hear an ordinary sound, and no longer feel the night closing in on him.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows sounds and fatigue as reminders that bring back the traumatic memory, but it does not clearly state that triggers themselves drive the memory in the required causal way within a paragraph.

Although reminders are present, the vignette does not explicitly show them causing Raymond's negative appraisals; it mainly says the reminders evoke fear and mistrust without a direct trigger-to-appraisal causal link.
The vignette states that mistrust shapes reactions to reminders and that sounds/situations stir the memory, but it does not clearly show negative appraisals causing the triggers/reminders themselves.
The vignette describes memory being brought back by sounds, but it does not also show the memory itself causing subsequent triggers/reminders in a causal chain.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette shows sounds and fatigue as reminders that bring back the traumatic memory, but it does not clearly state that triggers themselves drive the memory in the required causal way within a paragraph.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: Although reminders are present, the vignette does not explicitly show them causing Raymond's negative appraisals; it mainly says the reminders evoke fear and mistrust without a direct trigger-to-appraisal causal link.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette states that mistrust shapes reactions to reminders and that sounds/situations stir the memory, but it does not clearly show negative appraisals causing the triggers/reminders themselves.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette describes memory being brought back by sounds, but it does not also show the memory itself causing subsequent triggers/reminders in a causal chain.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
